article.headline: How to Prompt a Human: An Autistic Theory of Social Fluency
article.lede: A Twitter thread by @DefenderOfBasic argues that autistic people struggle socially not because they lack rules, but because the layer of rules they've studied is the wrong one. The proposed fix is to treat social interaction as a developer treats a language model: prompt, observe, predict, iterate. The metaphor turns out to have sharper academic backing than its self-help framing suggests.
article.body:
Pre-planned scripts for social interaction — the stock tool of skills training for autistic people — are “training wheels,” @DefenderOfBasic argues in a thread that has circulated widely. The problem isn't the scripts themselves but what they prevent: learning the underlying probabilistic grammar of human exchange. The thread borrows a concept from Stephen Wolfram to ground this claim. *Computational irreducibility*, developed in Wolfram's *A New Kind of Science* (2002), holds that certain systems — weather, cellular automata, perhaps conversation — have no mathematical shortcut; to find out what they'll do, you have to run every step they run. Scripts assume conversation is compressible. Wolfram's framework says it isn't.

What the thread proposes instead is a *Markov-chain* model of interaction. A Markov chain is a probabilistic system in which each state depends only on the immediately preceding state — not the full history. Applied here: given your current emotional state and the other person's reaction to it, the next conversational move is approximately predictable. The practical method is to enter a real exchange, try to prompt a specific response, predict what that response will be before it arrives, and update your internal model on what actually happens. The thread recommends emotionally charged online topics as a training ground, where the volume of interlocutors is large enough to separate genuine pattern from individual temperament. This is closer to empirical social science than therapy.

The research base is more supportive than the self-help framing suggests. Academic work by Choudhury and Basu at Microsoft (MSFT) Research formally validated the Markov-chain model of conversation, finding that turn-taking patterns measured from wearable sensors predicted social influence within group networks. And UCLA's **PEERS** program (*Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills*), the most rigorously validated social-skills intervention for autistic adults, arrives at a broadly similar conclusion about scripts: rigid verbal formulas don't generalize. PEERS instead uses role-play, peer observation, and structured analysis of what worked — something closer to the trial-and-error prompting the thread recommends.

The argument has real cracks, though. Wolfram's own framework is slightly self-undermining here: if social interaction is computationally irreducible, the Markov-chain approximation is precisely a shortcut — a reduction of what Wolfram says cannot be reduced. More substantially, a 2023 critical review found that autistic adults often already *possess* the relevant social knowledge; the bottleneck is real-time execution — speed, emotional processing, and flexible response generation. Knowing the grammar of a conversation is not the same as running it at 300-millisecond turn intervals. And a substantial literature on *masking* and *camouflaging* — the deliberate adaptive performance the thread recommends developing — consistently finds the strategy cognitively costly and associated with worse mental-health outcomes.

The thread also operates within a framework the field has increasingly questioned. The *double empathy problem*, first described by autistic researcher Damian Milton in 2012, argues that social difficulty between autistic and neurotypical people is bidirectional: a mismatch between two differently-disposed actors, not a unilateral autistic deficit. Supporting evidence: autistic people interact fluently with other autistic people; the friction arises specifically at the neurotypical interface. What the thread frames as a learnable skill — crack the human code — is, from this angle, adapting to an asymmetric interface where one side does all the translation. The thread's core practical insight survives: naturalistic practice and active prediction do beat scripts. The framing of it as a superpower, without reckoning with what the research shows it costs, does not.

concepts.definition: A concept from Stephen Wolfram's *A New Kind of Science* (2002). A computationally irreducible system is one where there is no mathematical shortcut to predict its future state: you must run every computational step the system itself runs. Wolfram argues many complex systems — weather, certain cellular automata, possibly human conversation — fall into this category, meaning any attempt to pre-model them is necessarily incomplete.

A probabilistic model in which a system moves between states, and each next state depends only on the current state — not on the full history of how it got there. The thread applies this to conversation: given two people's current emotional states and their most recent exchange, the next conversational move is approximately predictable from that snapshot alone, without needing to reconstruct the whole prior conversation.

Terms used in autism research for the deliberate, conscious strategies autistic people use to suppress autistic traits and conform to neurotypical social expectations. These include mirroring body language, using pre-planned phrases, suppressing visible stimming, and performing emotional attunement. Research consistently finds camouflaging cognitively costly and associated with burnout, anxiety, and reduced sense of authenticity.

A theory coined by autistic researcher Damian Milton in 2012 that reframes autistic social difficulty as mutual rather than unilateral. Where older theories (notably Simon Baron-Cohen's mind-blindness hypothesis) blamed autistic deficits in theory of mind, Milton argues the problem is a mismatch: autistic and neurotypical people misread each other in both directions. Key evidence: autistic people communicate fluently with other autistic people; difficulty arises specifically at the neurotypical interface.

The Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills, developed by Elizabeth Laugeson at UCLA. The most rigorously validated social-skills training program for autistic adolescents and adults, with randomized controlled trial evidence showing durable improvements in social knowledge, engagement frequency, and reduced symptoms. Unlike script-based approaches, PEERS uses role-play video analysis, group discussion of what worked, and naturalistic peer practice.

books.title: A New Kind of Science
books.author: Stephen Wolfram
books.summary: Published in 2002, Wolfram's 1,280-page treatise argues that simple computational rules — such as those governing cellular automata — can generate the complexity seen across the natural world. Its central contribution is the concept of computational irreducibility: for many systems, there is no shortcut to predicting future behavior; the system must simply be run. The book is controversial in academic physics and mathematics but has been influential in complexity theory and popular science writing about emergent phenomena.

article.fact_check: The thread invokes Wolfram's computational irreducibility to justify why scripts fail — the interaction can't be pre-computed — and then immediately proposes a Markov-chain model as the solution. These sit in tension: a Markov chain is a computationally *reducible* approximation; Wolfram's framework is precisely a claim that such approximations are incomplete for systems of sufficient complexity. The thread's practical advice survives this tension (naturalistic practice does outperform script rehearsal, per the PEERS literature), but the theoretical framing is internally inconsistent.
article.thread_summary: The two-part thread argues that autistic people who find social interaction confusing are trying to solve the wrong problem — memorizing surface rules rather than learning to model another person's emotional state in real time. The first part introduces the Wolfram / computational irreducibility framing to explain why scripts fail; the second recommends a specific practice method: prompt humans (especially online in emotionally charged discussions), predict their responses ahead of time, and iterate until the patterns become legible. The thread frames this as a transferable skill that translates from online to in-person interaction.
